title: Dementia and Hospice: Questions for an Individualized Evaluation
seoTitle: Dementia and Hospice: Questions for an Individualized Evaluation
description: Questions families can bring to an individualized dementia and hospice evaluation, including function, communication, eating, infections and goals of care.
lede: Dementia changes communication, routines and daily function in ways that can be difficult to describe. Families do not need to decide eligibility from a list of symptoms. A clinician or hospice team can review the person’s overall condition, changes over time, care needs and goals with the people who know the person best.
ctaHeading: Bring the questions to a clinician
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice can help families prepare for an individualized, physician-certified evaluation. Call 805.953.7273.

sections.heading: Start with the person’s changing daily life
paragraphs: A diagnosis of dementia does not by itself determine whether hospice is appropriate. The useful starting point is what has changed: communication, mobility, dressing, bathing, toileting, eating, sleeping, continence, safety or participation in familiar routines. Describe the difference between a month ago and today without trying to translate observations into a medical conclusion.

The National Institute on Aging explains that dementia affects thinking, memory and daily activities in different ways. In later-stage Alzheimer’s disease, people may need increasing help with daily activities, eating or swallowing, communication and personal care, and recurrent health complications can add to care needs. A family’s observations help the treating clinician understand the individual situation.

sections.heading: Notice patterns without turning them into a checklist
paragraphs: Families may notice increasing dependence, difficulty swallowing or chewing, recurrent infections, falls, weight or appetite changes, reduced communication or more frequent urgent visits. These observations deserve attention, but no single symptom qualifies someone for hospice. The team considers the whole picture and the patient’s goals.
Keep a short record of what happened, when it began and what help was needed. Include good days as well as difficult days. A pattern is more useful than a label applied to one event.

sections.heading: Communication and eating concerns deserve careful questions
paragraphs: A person with dementia may have difficulty finding words, following a conversation or explaining discomfort. Ask the clinician how the care team can learn what the person is trying to communicate and how preferences should be respected. If coughing, choking or swallowing changes occur, report them rather than changing food, fluids or medicines based on general advice.
Ask which concerns may have another treatable cause and how comfort, safety and the person’s wishes will guide decisions. The goal is not to force a choice but to make the next conversation clearer.

sections.heading: What an individualized evaluation may cover
paragraphs: A hospice evaluation may include recent infections or hospital visits, functional changes, symptoms, medications, eating and drinking, skin concerns, communication, caregiver capacity and the patient’s goals. The hospice may coordinate with the primary physician, specialist, facility staff and authorized decision-maker as appropriate.

Hospice eligibility is physician-certified and individualized. Requesting an evaluation is not a promise to enroll. If hospice is not the right fit at the time, ask what should be monitored and when it would make sense to revisit the conversation.

sections.heading: Questions for the family and care team
paragraphs: Ask the physician: What changes need clinical review? Which decisions should be documented now? What care remains available if hospice is not chosen? Ask the hospice: Who coordinates with the physician? What teaching and equipment may be available? How are after-hours concerns handled? How will the plan reflect the person’s values and communication style?

Bring the current medication list, names of clinicians, advance-care documents and a brief record of changes. The Family Guide and hospice evaluation guide can help organize questions before the call.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paragraphs: National Institute on Aging: Alzheimer’s and Dementia
National Institute on Aging: Late-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease
Medicare.gov: Hospice Care

title: Advanced Cancer and Hospice: Comfort-Focused Questions for Families
seoTitle: Advanced Cancer and Hospice: Comfort-Focused Questions for Families
description: A family guide to hospice conversations during advanced cancer, with questions about goals, symptoms, oncology coordination, equipment and care settings.
lede: Advanced cancer can bring changing treatment goals, difficult symptoms and many conversations with an oncology team. Hospice is one possible comfort-focused approach when it fits the patient’s wishes and clinical situation. This guide helps families prepare questions without telling them to stop treatment or predicting what will happen next.
ctaHeading: Make room for the patient’s questions
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice can explain the evaluation process while respecting the oncology team’s role. Call 805.953.7273.

sections.heading: Begin with goals, not assumptions
paragraphs: Ask what the patient most wants from care now: more time at home, relief from a troubling symptom, a family gathering, fewer disruptive trips or support for caregivers. Goals can change. A hospice conversation does not require the family to predict a date or make a decision before understanding the options.

The National Cancer Institute notes that advanced cancer is a broad term that may describe cancer that has spread or is unlikely to be cured. The oncology team remains central to explaining the patient’s diagnosis and treatment choices.

sections.heading: Keep communication open with oncology
paragraphs: The oncologist, primary physician and hospice team may each have a different role. Ask how information will be shared, which clinician manages current treatment questions and how a comfort-focused plan would coordinate with existing care. Do not stop, start or change cancer medicines because of an article or family discussion.

If treatment goals are changing, ask the oncology team what each option is intended to accomplish, what burdens it may bring and how it fits the patient’s priorities. Hospice can help organize questions while medical decisions remain individualized and physician-directed.

sections.heading: Describe symptom burden specifically
paragraphs: Report pain, nausea, breathlessness, fatigue, anxiety, poor appetite, sleep changes or other concerns to the treating team. A short record can include when a symptom occurs, how it affects an activity, what the patient says and which clinician has been contacted. Do not prescribe a remedy for yourself or change medication instructions without clinical guidance.

Ask the hospice what number to call, what information to have ready and how the team will respond when a symptom changes. The plan may include teaching and comfort-focused medications under physician direction.

sections.heading: Ask about home support and setting
paragraphs: Hospice may provide care where the person lives, including a private home, assisted living or skilled nursing setting. Ask how planned visits work, which team members may be involved, what caregiver teaching is available and whether equipment related to the hospice plan could help. Services and coverage depend on the patient’s plan and payer, so confirm details rather than assuming.
Hospice is not continuous bedside nursing. On-call support is available for questions and coordination, while emergencies should follow the patient’s emergency plan and local emergency guidance.

sections.heading: Questions before an evaluation
paragraphs: Ask: What changes should we report? How will hospice coordinate with oncology? Which services are included in the proposed plan? What equipment or medication questions should we resolve? Who should be included in updates? What happens if the patient’s goals change? These questions make space for the patient’s voice and the family’s real capacity.
The evaluation guide and Family Guide can help prepare. Requesting information does not obligate a patient to enroll.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paragraphs: National Cancer Institute: Advanced Cancer
Medicare.gov: Hospice Care

title: Advanced Heart Failure and Hospice: Planning Around Changing Needs
seoTitle: Advanced Heart Failure and Hospice: Planning Around Changing Needs
description: Questions for families planning around advanced heart failure, including changing function, symptom reporting, cardiology coordination and caregiver needs.
lede: Advanced heart failure can include better days and difficult days, making it hard for families to know when to ask for additional support. A hospice conversation is not an automatic response to one hospitalization. It is an opportunity to discuss changing needs, patient goals and how cardiology, primary care, caregivers and hospice may coordinate.
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice can help families prepare questions about advanced heart failure and an individualized evaluation. Call 805.953.7273.

sections.heading: Look at function and the changing pattern
paragraphs: The American Heart Association notes that heart failure symptoms and functional effects vary among individuals. Families may observe more fatigue, breathlessness, swelling, reduced stamina, trouble sleeping comfortably or increasing help with ordinary activities. These observations do not establish hospice eligibility. Share them with the treating clinician.
Keep a brief record of daily function, symptoms, clinician-directed measurements and recent hospital or emergency visits. Include fluctuations rather than describing only the hardest day.

sections.heading: Coordinate with cardiology and primary care
paragraphs: The cardiology and primary care teams can explain current treatment goals, medicines, devices and what changes should be reported. Ask how a hospice evaluation would fit with those relationships and who will communicate updates. Never stop or adjust heart failure medicines because of general information.
A hospice team can add support for comfort, caregiver teaching and practical planning when appropriate. It does not replace the clinicians responsible for individualized medical decisions.

sections.heading: Make symptom reporting specific
paragraphs: Report worsening breathlessness, fatigue, swelling, confusion, dizziness, appetite changes or a notable change in function to the clinical team. Ask which signs require a call, which number to use after hours and what information to have ready. Follow the patient’s documented emergency plan when emergency services are needed.

A written plan can reduce uncertainty, but no article can determine whether a symptom is an emergency or predict the illness course. The patient’s clinicians should give guidance for the individual situation.

sections.heading: Discuss equipment and medication questions
paragraphs: Ask whether equipment related to the hospice plan could make transfers, bathing or rest safer. A hospital bed, commode, oxygen or other item may or may not be appropriate; the clinical team decides with the patient and caregivers. Confirm coverage and arrangements before relying on a service.

Ask who manages refills, how the hospice coordinates with cardiology and what to do when swallowing, alertness or daily function changes. Keep the medication list current and do not make changes without instructions.

sections.heading: Include caregiver capacity and patient goals
paragraphs: Ask what a good day means to the patient and what burdens the patient hopes to avoid. Discuss who can be present, which tasks are realistic and whether hospitalization would match the patient’s goals if the condition worsens. These conversations can be revisited as wishes and capacity change.
The evaluation guide and Family Guide can help organize questions for a physician or hospice. Asking for information is not an enrollment decision.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paragraphs: American Heart Association: Heart Failure
Medicare.gov: Hospice Care

title: Advanced COPD and Hospice: Questions About Comfort and Breathing Changes
seoTitle: Advanced COPD and Hospice: Questions About Comfort and Breathing Changes
description: A practical family guide to questions about advanced COPD, changing breathing symptoms, comfort-focused support, equipment and caregiver planning.
lede: Advanced COPD can make ordinary activities more demanding and can bring periods of worsening breathing, fatigue or recovery after an exacerbation. Families do not need to interpret an oxygen reading or decide eligibility on their own. A clinician or hospice team can help connect observed changes with the patient’s goals and an appropriate plan.
ctaCopy: Eternal Life Hospice can answer questions about advanced COPD, comfort planning and an individualized evaluation. Call 805.953.7273.

sections.heading: Describe changes in daily life
paragraphs: The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute explains that COPD can affect breathing and ordinary activities. Families may notice less activity tolerance, more fatigue, appetite or weight changes, recurrent infections, more help with bathing or dressing or longer recovery after a flare. Share trends with the treating clinician; no single observation determines hospice eligibility.
Record what the person can do, what has changed and when. Include the patient’s own description of breathlessness and the activities that matter most.

sections.heading: Ask when and how to call
paragraphs: Breathing changes can be frightening. Ask the clinician and hospice team which changes require a call, which number to use after hours and what information to have ready. Hospice provides on-call guidance and coordination, but it is not continuous bedside nursing. For urgent symptom changes related to the terminal illness, call the hospice team first unless the patient’s care plan directs otherwise. Follow the patient’s emergency plan when emergency services are needed.
This article cannot tell a family whether a particular episode is an emergency or provide independent treatment instructions.

sections.heading: Keep oxygen and medicines clinician-directed
paragraphs: Ask the prescribing clinician how oxygen, inhaled medicines and other treatments fit the patient’s plan. Do not change oxygen settings, start medicines or stop medicines based on general advice. If swallowing, alertness, anxiety or symptom severity changes, report it to the clinical team.
Hospice may provide caregiver teaching and coordinate physician-directed comfort measures. What is appropriate depends on the patient’s condition, equipment and goals.

sections.heading: Plan for comfort and caregiver teaching
paragraphs: Ask the team how it will assess breathlessness, anxiety, sleep, fatigue, cough and the effect of symptoms on daily life. Families can ask for clear demonstrations, written instructions and a plan for medication questions. Equipment related to the hospice plan may be considered for the person’s setting, but the clinical team decides what is appropriate.

Keep pathways clear, place important phone numbers where caregivers can find them and discuss who can help when the primary caregiver needs a break. Practical planning should fit the household’s real capacity.

sections.heading: Questions for an individualized evaluation
paragraphs: Ask: What changes should we report? How will hospice coordinate with pulmonary care and primary care? Which equipment and teaching may be available? Who answers after-hours questions? What does the patient want during a difficult breathing episode? What support remains available if hospice is not selected now?

Requesting an evaluation does not force enrollment. Eligibility is individualized and physician-certified. The Family Guide and evaluation guide can help the family prepare without turning observations into a checklist.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paragraphs: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute: COPD
Medicare.gov: Hospice Care

title: After Hospice Starts: A Family’s First 48 Hours
seoTitle: After Hospice Starts: A Family’s First 48 Hours
description: A calm first-48-hours checklist for families after hospice begins, covering the first visit, the care plan, supplies, calls and caregiver questions.
lede: The first two days after hospice begins can bring new names, instructions, supplies and emotions. Families do not need to master everything at once. Use this short timeline to know what to gather, what to ask and when to call, while keeping the patient’s goals at the center.

sections.heading: At the first visit: make the plan clear
paragraphs: The first visit is a chance to listen, assess comfort and agree on practical next steps. Keep the patient’s medication list, allergies, clinician names, advance-care documents and preferred contacts nearby. Tell the nurse what the patient wants protected, which tasks feel difficult and what the household can realistically do.

Ask who is the main hospice contact, which number to use after hours, when the next planned visit is expected and how updates will be shared with the attending physician. Request plain-language explanations and write down names, phone numbers and questions that can wait for the next visit.

sections.heading: During day one: check the essentials
paragraphs: Ask what medications, supplies or equipment relate to the plan of care and what the household should do while an item is being arranged. Timing can vary, so ask which needs are most important to report first. Do not start, stop or change medicines, diets, oxygen or equipment settings without clinician direction.

Walk through the patient’s usual space. Keep the call number, medication list, water and needed personal items easy to find. Clear a safe path without removing objects that make the room familiar. Tell the team if a transfer, bathroom routine or caregiving task feels unsafe.

sections.heading: At any hour: know how to call
paragraphs: Hospice offers 24/7 on-call support for questions and urgent symptom guidance. On-call support is not continuous bedside nursing and does not promise an instant arrival. Ask what information to share, who answers after hours and what the documented care plan says about emergency services.

For urgent symptom changes related to the terminal illness, call the hospice team first unless the patient’s care plan directs otherwise. Follow the patient’s emergency plan when emergency services are needed. If a situation appears life-threatening, use the patient’s documented emergency instructions and tell responders about hospice involvement.

sections.heading: By the second day: make the checklist usable
paragraphs: Keep one shared note with the hospice number, the patient’s priorities, questions, meaningful changes and the guidance received. One caregiver can write while another stays with the patient. Include the patient in teaching and decisions as much as possible, and identify a backup contact if the primary caregiver needs rest.

The plan can be revisited. Ask the team to explain anything that remains unclear, including visit roles, equipment teaching, medication questions and who coordinates with the physician. A family does not need to solve every future decision during the first 48 hours; it needs a clear next call and a realistic plan for today.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paragraphs: Medicare.gov: Hospice Care
CMS: Hospice Care Coverage

title: Can a Family Request a Hospice Evaluation?
seoTitle: Can a Family Request a Hospice Evaluation?
description: Yes, families can ask for hospice information and an evaluation. Learn who participates, what happens next, and how physician certification guides care.
lede: A family does not have to wait for a physician to raise hospice before asking questions. You can contact a hospice to request information or an evaluation, then invite the patient’s physician and other clinicians into the conversation. The evaluation is individualized, and hospice eligibility is physician-certified where required. Asking for an evaluation is not the same as enrolling; it is a practical way to understand choices before a crisis.

sections.heading: What a family can ask for
paragraphs: You can ask a hospice to explain its services, service area, response process, and evaluation steps. You can share what has changed: more help with daily activities, repeated hospital visits, declining appetite, worsening symptoms, or caregiver exhaustion. A hospice may request permission to contact the patient’s physician and obtain clinical information. The patient’s privacy and decision-making rights remain central.

If the patient can make decisions, include them in the conversation as much as possible. If someone else is authorized to decide, identify that person and gather advance directive or health care representative documents. Family concern matters, but a family member cannot enroll a capable patient over that person’s wishes. Ask the hospice to explain who must sign and what choices remain available.

sections.heading: What happens during an evaluation
paragraphs: A nurse reviews the illness history, recent changes, medicines, function, safety, symptoms, living situation, and goals. The team may coordinate with the attending physician and hospice medical director. The conversation should make room for questions about treatment, hospitalization, equipment, caregiver teaching, after-hours calls, and emotional support.

Eligibility is not based on a diagnosis name alone. The physician-certified determination considers the complete picture and applicable hospice requirements. If the person is eligible and wants hospice, the hospice explains election and creates a plan of care. If not, ask what changes should prompt another evaluation and whether other supportive services may be appropriate.

sections.heading: How to prepare before calling
paragraphs: Make a one-page summary. Include the diagnosis as the physician has described it, recent hospital or emergency visits, noticeable functional changes, falls or infections, eating and drinking changes, symptoms, current medicines, and the names of clinicians. Include the patient’s priorities in their own words: staying home, remaining alert, attending an event, or avoiding certain interventions.

You do not need perfect records. Honest observations are useful. “She now needs help getting from bed to the bathroom” is more helpful than “she is declining.” Note dates when possible, but do not delay a call while searching for every detail. The hospice team can tell you what information it needs and how to obtain missing records.

sections.heading: Questions for comparing hospice providers
paragraphs: Ask who is available after hours, how visits are scheduled, how the team communicates with physicians, and what happens when symptoms change. Ask whether the hospice serves the patient’s home, assisted living community, or skilled nursing setting. Ask how caregivers are taught, what equipment may be coordinated, and how bereavement support works.

Confirm coverage with the hospice and insurer. Benefits and patient responsibility can vary; do not assume hospice is free or that every service is covered. Ask specifically about medications, equipment, supplies, respite, and services unrelated to the hospice plan. A transparent provider will explain what it knows and help identify questions for the payer.

sections.heading: The value of asking early
paragraphs: An evaluation can reduce the pressure of making decisions in an emergency. It gives families time to hear the patient’s wishes, identify a decision-maker, organize the home, and understand how to reach support. It may also reveal that hospice is not yet the right fit. Either outcome is useful when the family has a clearer plan.

Families and referral partners across Ventura and Los Angeles Counties can begin with a simple question: “Could you help us understand whether hospice might fit this situation?” The answer should be respectful, specific, and free of pressure. Care planning works best when concerns are heard early and revisited as the person’s needs change.

sections.heading: Keep the plan personal
paragraphs: There is no universal “right” way to live with advanced illness. One person may value quiet mornings at home; another may prioritize visits, faith practices, or time with grandchildren. Tell the team about routines, language preferences, cultural practices, and the people who should be included. These details are not extras. They help clinicians make recommendations that fit real life.

Asking for help is an act of advocacy. Keep notes, bring questions, and speak up when instructions are unclear. The hospice team should explain what it can do, what it cannot do, and whom to call next.

For referral partners, a warm handoff can make the first call easier. Tell the family why you are recommending a conversation, confirm permission to share contact information, and note urgent concerns clearly. The hospice team can then coordinate with the physician and explain next steps. Good communication protects continuity while leaving the patient and authorized decision-maker in control.

Comfort-focused care is personal and culturally grounded. Invite the patient to describe important foods, music, people, rituals, and places. The team can document preferences and discuss what is medically safe within the plan. Respectful care does not require a family to have the same beliefs or coping style; it requires room for each person to be heard.

Families often wait for certainty that no one can provide. Instead, look for a clear next step: call the physician, request an evaluation, update the medication list, or identify the decision-maker. Small preparations create room for better conversations. If circumstances change, the family can return to the hospice team and ask for guidance again.
